CPDP 2027

The governance of the digital world is fragmented and faces difficult challenges. Technologies that shape our lives develop faster than the means – or even the will – to regulate them for the protection of privacy and other fundamental rights.
What We Owe the Future invites reflection on this contribution. Building on this, it looks ahead to what the future demands of us. What will the next twenty or more years need, and how should we help to build it? What do we owe to those who will inherit the world we shape today? Which principles must endure, which protections cannot be bargained away even when the pressure to relax them is strong, and what responsibilities do the custodians of the present bear towards the future?
The year 2027 marks the twentieth anniversary of CPDP. For twenty years, the conferences have stood at the forefront of efforts to understand and contribute to improving the prospect for governance in this fast-moving digital age. As a community of academics, regulators and policymakers, civil society, industry and legal practitioners, CPDP has cast a bright light on issues, practices and rules, and has offered a forum for debate and the exchange of knowledge across a global landscape. What is worth celebrating is not the annual conference itself, but twenty years of bringing this community together and sustaining it through a period of momentous change.
The people whose lives will extend far into that future should help to design the way forward. CPDP 2027 therefore launches CPDP 20: The Next Generation, which include a team of early-career researchers from across disciplineswho will co-curate the programme and help identify its most pressing questions. This team will identify connections across fields and help to explore issues on the horizon, bringing knowledge and fresh perspectives to bear on developments and their likely consequences that will need to be addressed by policy, governance and other action.

title: First harmonised standard supporting the AI Act published in the Official Journal
text:
The standard, EN 18286:2026 - Artificial intelligence - Quality management system for EU AI Act regulatory purposes, developed by CEN and CENELEC, provides a clear legal pathway for providers of high-risk AI systems to comply with the quality management system requirements under article 17 of the AI Act.
Its publication through Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2026/2274 means that providers implementing this standard will benefit from a presumption of conformity with the Article 17 requirements covered by the standard.
EN 18286 translates these requirements into an operational quality management system (QMS). It is the only AI QMS standard with a presumption of conformity. It is mapped to Article 17 of the AI Act, built around the AI system lifecycle – rather than the organisation – and designed to be layered on top of the existing international standards – such as ISO/IEC 42001, ISO 9001 or a sectoral QMS (e.g. ISO 13485) – rather than replace them. 
EN 18286 explicitly allows providers in regulated sectors to integrate management systems, rather than run separate ones. Organisations without ISO/IEC 42001 that plan to place or put into service high-risk AI systems in the EU market can use EN 18286 to expand an existing QMS or build one that fulfills the requirements of article 17 requirements.
The publication of this standard marks an important milestone in implementing the AI Act, ahead of the application of requirements for high-risk AI systems, with further harmonised standards expected to follow.
Find further information about the Standardisation of the AI Act.

title: CVE-2026-76788 - Stack out-of-bounds write in the OSDP Control Panel reply parser
text:
8.8

HIGH
CVSS 3.1

CVE-2026-76788
Stack out-of-bounds write in the OSDP Control Panel reply parser

The OSDP Control Panel reply parser cp_decode_response() in subsys/mgmt/osdp/src/osdp_cp.c decodes replies from a Peripheral Device into a stack-allocated struct osdp_event. For the REPLY_KEYPPAD and REPLY_RAW reply types, the payload length is taken from the received frame and the only validation performed is that the declared length is self-consistent with the number of payload bytes present in the frame. Because the attacker controls both the length field and the frame length, that check imposes no bound, and the subsequent memcpy() writes into the fixed 64-byte data arrays of struct osdp_event_keypress / struct osdp_event_cardread (OSDP_EVENT_MAX_DATALEN). The sibling REPLY_FMT handler in the same switch already carried the missing > OSDP_EVENT_MAX_DATALEN bound.

The defect is reached from cp_process_reply(), which reads bytes from the OSDP RS-485 channel and passes them through osdp_phy_check_packet() and osdp_phy_decode_packet() before dispatching on the reply ID. Triggering it requires CONFIG_OSDP with CONFIG_OSDP_MODE_CP and an application event callback registered (the normal Control Panel integration), plus a frame carrying a correct SOM, a valid CRC-16, and a matching 2-bit sequence number — all of which are computable or observable by anyone on the bus. No check ties the reply ID to the outstanding command, so an oversized REPLY_KEYPPAD or REPLY_RAW is accepted as the answer to a routine CMD_POLL. A malicious or compromised card reader, or anyone with access to the RS-485 wiring, can supply such a frame; CONFIG_OSDP_SC_ENABLED only helps while a secure channel is active, and a single unauthenticated frame carrying a bad MAC causes sc_deactivate(), after which plaintext replies are again accepted.

With the default CONFIG_OSDP_UART_BUFFER_LENGTH of 256, roughly 180 bytes of fully attacker-chosen data can be written past the end of the stack-allocated event object, over saved registers and the return address on typical Cortex-M and RISC-V frame layouts (Zephyr does not enable stack canaries by default). The impact ranges from a hard crash of the access-control panel to potential control-flow hijack in the context of the OSDP receive thread. The fix adds an OSDP_EVENT_MAX_DATALEN bound to both handlers, capping each memcpy() at the size of its destination.

title: CVE-2026-112393 - Pillow: Heap buffer overflow in _tiffWriteProc when saving TIFF to BytesIO
text:
9.2

CRITICAL
CVSS 4.0

CVE-2026-112393
Pillow: Heap buffer overflow in _tiffWriteProc when saving TIFF to BytesIO

Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 2.0.0 until 13.0.0, Pillow has a heap buffer overflow and stale-heap disclosure in _tiffWriteProc when saving compressed TIFF data through libtiff to a target without a usable fileno(), such as BytesIO. The callback sizes its allocation from the prior buffer size instead of the current write position, allowing an attacker-controlled out-of-line TIFF tag or retained ICC profile to be copied beyond the allocation after libtiff seeks forward. This overflow can crash the process and may allow code execution. Independently, unwritten alignment gaps in compressed TIFF output larger than 64 KiB can disclose stale heap bytes without a crafted tag. File paths and targets with real file descriptors are unaffected. This issue is fixed in version 13.0.0.

CVE-2026-53995
MLflow 3.17.1 Path Traversal via Trace ID API

MLflow 3.17.1 and earlier contains a path traversal vulnerability in the FileStore tracking backend that allows unauthenticated attackers to control filesystem paths by submitting a crafted trace ID containing traversal sequences to the POST /api/3.0/mlflow/traces endpoint. Threat actors have begun to exploit a chain of vulnerabilities in Plex Media Server to deploy cryptocurrency miners and reverse proxy software, a day after a proof-of-concept (PoC) went public.

According to a researcher who goes by the online alias boredhackerblog, the exploitation activity involves chaining four different vulnerabilities, collectively called Plex2Shell.

The vulnerabilities are below -

CVE-2026-96652 (CVSS score: 5.3) - An unauthenticated server-side request forgery (SSRF) stemming via the "/player/timeline" endpoint by taking advantage of the fact that the "protocol" parameter is inserted into a programmatically-constructed player URL with no validation, allowing an attacker to force the Plex server to POST to a destination of their choice.
CVE-2026-96654 (CVSS score: 6.9) - An improper neutralization of URL values included in the "searchOne" endpoint that could allow an attacker to call other plugins' functions and supply their own parameters to obtain the owner's admin token.
CVE-2026-96655 (CVSS score: 5.3) - An SSRF vulnerability that allows an authenticated user (i.e., the owner token) to request arbitrary internal or external addresses (e.g., an attacker-hosted carrier video carrying the malicious ELF payload) via the '/video/:/transcode/universal' path parameter.
CVE-2026-96656 (CVSS score: 8.6) - An external control of file name or path vulnerability that allows the ELF shared object to an attacker-chosen path in the Codecs directory and execute it.

Put differently, the vulnerabilities can be combined together in this order to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution on susceptible Plex Media Server instances.

The vulnerabilities, along with CVE-2026-96651 (CVSS score: 7.1), were disclosed to Plex on July 27, 2026, by security researcher Zach Main, and were patched in Plex Media Server 1.43.3.10861 released on August 3, 2026.

In-the-wild exploitation attempts targeting the flaws have since been recorded a day after technical details of the Plex2Shell chain went public on October 16, 2026. The attacks led to the deployment of a miner payload from a remote server ("217.60.194[.]116").

The attack efforts have been observed from the following IP addresses -

91.92.40[.]202
176.65.139[.]228
45.194.92[.]222
176.65.139[.]228

Furthermore, the vulnerabilities have been exploited to deliver an artifact named "myawesomeproxy," which, according to VirusTotal, is a stealthy Linux backdoor and reverse proxy. Running the program displays the below message, per boredhackerblog -

Running this software on any of your devices makes you agree to the potential external use of your internet traffic.

Also deployed concurrently is an XMRig miner process identified as "mylovelyminer" with its mining server pointing to "ota.proxystream[.]st." Notably, another subdomain associated with the same domain, "global.relay.proxystream[.]st," was flagged by Bitsight in August 2026 in connection with the AISURU DDoS and proxyware botnet.

Posts on Reddit indicate that multiple Plex users have had their instances compromised with the same "mylovelyminer" payload. That said, it's not known at this stage if it stems from the exploitation of Plex2Shell flaws.

The development comes more than a month after Plex urged users to update their instances to the latest version following the release of an update that addressed multiple unspecified security flaws.

Copies of Rank Math PRO, the paid version of the Rank Math SEO plugin for WordPress, that were downloaded from rankmath.com or delivered as updates between 20:02 UTC on October 15 and 07:12 UTC on October 16 contained malware, Rank Math said in a security notice published on October 16.

Any site that installed and activated one of those copies should be treated as compromised, and the malware can recreate its hidden backdoor whenever someone visits the site.

Rank Math has removed the affected files and released a clean version, 3.0.124. Installing it replaces the plugin but does not remove files, administrator accounts, or scheduled tasks the malware may already have placed elsewhere on the server, Wordfence said in an advisory on October 17.

Who Is Affected

The version number does not show whether a copy is affected. Rank Math's changelog dates 3.0.123 to October 7, more than a week before the window opened, and the notice limits the incident to copies downloaded or installed through an update during the window.

A copy of 3.0.123 obtained before 20:02 UTC on October 15 is outside it.

The notice sorts sites into three cases:

You installed and activated 3.0.123 during the window: treat the site as compromised, even if it has since been updated to 3.0.124, and follow the recovery steps below.
You installed it but never activated it: delete the plugin files, install 3.0.124 from your Rank Math account, and run a security scan.
You downloaded it but never installed or activated it: nothing in this incident alone indicates the site was compromised.

Rank Math has emailed some users about the incident and told anyone unsure whether the files were installed or activated to contact its support team.

The notice applies only to the PRO plugin, which customers download and update from rankmath.com rather than WordPress.org. The free Rank Math SEO plugin on WordPress.org, which lists more than 4 million active installations and was last updated on October 6, is not named in it.

What the Malware Does

What is known about the malware comes from Rank Math's notice. Neither it nor Wordfence's advisory includes an analysis of the code, and neither names who is behind it.

Deleting suspicious files before stopping what recreates the backdoor may not resolve the problem, which is why the cleanup order below matters. The attacker may also have left PHP backdoor files in other plugins' folders, in theme folders, and in the must-use plugins directory, created administrator accounts, added a fake WordPress core file, changed .htaccess so that .cache files run as PHP, and added scheduled tasks and SSH keys.

Any password, database credential, API key, or other secret the site could reach may have been exposed, and owners should assume it was.

Wordfence assigned the incident CVE-2026-111862 and rates it 9.8 out of 10, with the researcher listed as unknown.

Patchstack classifies it as a backdoor and says that, because the attack was on Rank Math's own systems, "a rule is not possible for mitigation."

How to Recover

Rank Math's preferred recovery is a restore. Where a backup of the site and its database from before 20:02 UTC on October 15 exists, restore it, run a security scan, change every password and credential, and only then install 3.0.124 from your Rank Math account.

Where no clean backup exists, the manual cleanup runs in a fixed order, and three actions come before anything else is touched:

Delete the entire rank-math-pro plugin folder using the hosting file manager or FTP. "Deactivating the plugin alone is not sufficient," the notice says.

title: Beyond the patch: Protecting your NetScaler gateway against future vulnerabilities
text: The recent disclosure of a major vulnerability in Citrix NetScaler pointed to a widespread weak point: a login page is an attack surface that can be used to compromise and access an application server. Indeed, the disclosures included an actively exploited flaw that allowed attackers to execute commands on affected gateways without signing in. As with any emergency patch, admins had to weigh cutting off or disrupting their users’ access with the risk of delaying a critical security update.If you’re a NetScaler customer and you haven’t patched your instance, stop reading and go do that. This was a bad one. Once you’ve finished the patch, we’ll explore how to avoid a future fire drill by laying additional security controls.This issue extends beyond NetScaler and can be applied to any internal application available on the Internet. Remote desktop portals, administrative consoles, and other publicly accessible authentication pages all deserve the same scrutiny: Does the intended audience require unrestricted Internet reachability? And can an attacker bypass this authentication check to reach the application's server?Citrix released software updates to address the flaw, and Cloudflare followed with an emergency web application firewall (WAF) rule on October 1. But having a patch available does not guarantee safety: every instance has to be identified, updated, and tested. Applying updates across a production deployment is painful — it can result in downtime or cause disruptions to employees who still need their desktops throughout that process. Customers, patients, and others dependent on users of a remote desktop definitely don’t care about your security patch.Using a web application firewall (WAF) can buy some additional time before a patch can be fully rolled out, but it’s reactive and does not account for the next exploit that’s discovered. Cloudflare and other security vendors do their best to cover variations and similar attacks. But AI is hastening how rapidly attackers can discover new and novel variants. That’s why it is crucial to build defense in depth, to ensure that no specific software failure or exploit will lead to a critical security issue.Cloudflare combines access policies, web application security, and restricted origin connections to protect the authentication service before a new vulnerability is disclosed. Access controls limit who can reach the application server; WAF inspection evaluates web requests for attacks; origin restrictions prevent direct connections from bypassing those defenses. These reduce exposure without waiting for a new exploit signature or replacing the existing desktop platform.Copy linkThe NetScaler exploitCitrix's September 27, 2026 bulletin reported observed exploitation of CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772. The first allows unauthenticated command execution on affected appliances, including in their default configuration. The second affects configurations using Datagram Transport Layer Security, or DTLS. Further advisories on October 3 and October 8 addressed additional vulnerabilities in SAML configurations. These exploits allowed attackers to execute arbitrary scripts on target machines and also execute denial of service attacks.CISA's alert and Mandiant's technical investigation cover the vulnerabilities, observed exploitation, and response guidance in more detail. For details of the available web application protection, see Cloudflare's emergency WAF release for CVE-2026-88771.In a typical Citrix deployment, the user authenticates through NetScaler Gateway, which then uses a secure ticket authority to pass through to the StoreFront, which presents the applications and desktops available to that user. The native-installed Citrix app then uses that information to establish a separate connection using Citrix's Independent Computing Architecture (ICA) protocol. CVE-2026-13762 and CVE-2026-13763 - Issue with HTTP/2 multi-frame request body inspection in AWS WAF

Bulletin ID: 2026-048-AWS
Scope: AWS
Content Type: Important (requires attention)
Publication Date: 06/29/2026 13:15 PM PDT

Description:

AWS WAF is a web application firewall that monitors the HTTP(S) requests that are forwarded to your protected web application resources. We identified CVE-2026-13762 and CVE-2026-13763, which are issues affecting HTTP/2 multi-frame request body inspection by AWS WAF.

CVE-2026-13762 affects AWS WAF deployment with CloudFront. This issue was remediated server-side; no customer action is required.

CVE-2026-13763 affects AWS WAF deployment with AWS Application Load Balancer (ALB). Under certain conditions, a crafted multi-frame HTTP/2 request could cause only a partial request body to be inspected. This issue has been addressed on ALB, and customers can ensure full protection by configuring how AWS WAF inspects HTTP/2 request bodies on their ALB.

Resolution:

On May 22, 2026, we released a new configuration option on ALB, which addresses this issue. We recommend that customers review and update the WAF HTTP/2 traffic inspection behavior under target group attributes for HTTP/2 endpoints. This enables ALB to accumulate HTTP/2 data frames before AWS WAF performs inspection. For detailed instructions, refer to the developer guide.

Workarounds:

No workarounds are available.

CVE-2026-13763

We would like to thank Kyungrok Choi, Woonghee Lee, and Junbeom Hur from Korea University ISSLab for collaborating on these issues through the coordinated vulnerability disclosure process.

Bulletin ID: 2026-021-AWS
Scope: AWS
Content Type: Important (requires attention)
Publication Date: 04/29/2026 11:45 AM PDT

Description:

CVE-2026-7422: Insufficient packet validation in the IPv4 and IPv6 receive paths allows an adjacent network device to send a packet that bypasses checksum and minimum-size validation by spoofing the Ethernet source MAC address to match one of the target device's own registered endpoints.

CVE-2026-7422 (ICMP integer underflow) can be mitigated by disabling outgoing ping support by setting ipconfigSUPPORT_OUTGOING_PINGS to 0 in your FreeRTOSIPConfig.h configuration file, or by updating to a fixed version. CVE-2026-8596 & CVE-2026-8597: Issue with Amazon SageMaker Python SDK - Model artifact integrity verification issues

Bulletin ID: 2026-031-AWS
Scope: AWS
Content Type: Important (requires attention)
Publication Date: 05/14/2026 12:45 PM PDT

Description:

Amazon SageMaker Python SDK is an open-source library for training and deploying machine learning models on Amazon SageMaker. The ModelBuilder component simplifies model deployment by automating model artifact preparation and SageMaker model creation.

We identified two issues affecting the model artifact integrity verification mechanism in the ModelBuilder/Serve component:

CVE-2026-8596: We identified a cleartext storage of sensitive information issue in the ModelBuilder/Serve component. When building models using ModelBuilder, the SDK stored an HMAC signing key as a container environment variable (SAGEMAKER_SERVE_SECRET_KEY). This key was returned in plaintext by SageMaker describe APIs (DescribeModel, DescribeEndpointConfig, DescribeModelPackage). A remote authenticated actor with permissions to call these APIs and S3 write access to the model artifact path could extract the key, forge valid integrity signatures for specially crafted model artifacts, and achieve code execution in inference containers.

CVE-2026-8597: We identified a missing integrity verification issue in the Triton inference handler. The Triton handler deserialized model artifacts without performing integrity verification before execution. A remote authenticated actor with S3 write access to the model artifact path could replace model artifacts with a specially crafted pickle payload that would be deserialized without verification, achieving code execution in inference containers.

Impacted versions: Amazon SageMaker Python SDK >= v2.199.0 AND <= v2.257.1, >= v3.0.0 AND <= v3.7.1

Resolution:

These issues have been addressed in Amazon SageMaker Python SDK v2.257.2 and v3.8.0. We recommend upgrading to the latest version and rebuilding any models previously created with ModelBuilder using the updated SDK. Models created with affected versions may still have the HMAC key stored in their container environment variables until they are rebuilt with the patched SDK.

Workarounds:

If upgrading is not immediately possible, users can manually remove the SAGEMAKER_SERVE_SECRET_KEY environment variable from existing SageMaker models by recreating the model without this variable in the container environment configuration. Additionally, users should restrict S3 write access to model artifact paths to only trusted principals.

CVE-2026-8597

Bulletin ID: 2026-056-AWS
Scope: AWS
Content Type: Important (requires attention)
Publication Date: 07/15/2026 11:30 AM PDT

Description:

Strands Agents is an open-source Python SDK for building and running AI agents. The strands-agents-tools package provides pre-built tools for use with the SDK, including the elasticsearch_memory tool for agent memory storage. We identified CVE-2026-15746, a server-side request forgery (SSRF) issue in the elasticsearch_memory tool. The tool exposed its connection parameters (es_url, cloud_id, api_key) as fields the large language model (LLM) could control through the tool schema. This issue has been addressed in strands-agents-tools version 0.7.0. We recommend upgrading to the latest version and ensuring any forked or derivative code is patched to incorporate the new fixes. As a precautionary measure, we recommend all operators rotate their ELASTICSEARCH_API_KEY, even if there is no indication the credential was exposed.

Workarounds:

Avoid using the elasticsearch_memory tool until you upgrade to version 0.7.0 or later. If you must continue running an affected version, do not expose the ELASTICSEARCH_API_KEY environment variable to the tool, and restrict outbound network access so the agent host can reach only your trusted Elasticsearch endpoint.

Scope: AWS

Description:

containerd is an open-source container runtime used by Kubernetes via the Container Runtime Interface (CRI) plugin. It underpins AWS managed container services including Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS), AWS Fargate, Bottlerocket, and Amazon Linux. AWS identified five issues in the containerd CRI plugin affecting versions 1.7 through 2.3

CVE-2026-16317 and CVE-2026-16318: Issues with s2n-tls: an open-source implementation of the TLS/SSL protocols

Bulletin ID: 2026-062-AWS
Scope: AWS
Content Type: Important (requires attention)
Publication Date: 07/21/2026 13:00 PM PDT

Description:

s2n-tls is an open source C99 implementation of the TLS/SSL protocol. We have identified two distinct issues:

CVE-2026-16317: Silent Drop of TLS 1.3 Encrypted Records in s2n-tls
Missing validation of the outer content_type byte on TLS 1.3 encrypted records in s2n-tls allows an active man-in-the-middle to silently drop individual application data records without either endpoint detecting the modification. RFC 8446 Section 5.2 requires that the outer content_type of all encrypted TLS 1.3 records must be application_data (0x17). The s2n-tls AEAD implementation hardcodes this value in the additional authenticated data rather than using the actual wire byte, so the outer content_type is not covered by the authentication tag. All TLS 1.3 connections are affected. Both TLS clients and servers are affected. TLS 1.2 and QUIC connections are not affected.

CVE-2026-16318: QUIC Transport Parameters Memory Leak During HelloRetryRequest in s2n-tls
Incorrect use of s2n_alloc instead of s2n_realloc in the QUIC transport parameters extension handler in s2n-tls causes one memory allocation to be leaked each time a QUIC-enabled TLS 1.3 connection goes through a HelloRetryRequest. This can occur during normal handshakes when a client offers a key share group the server does not prefer, and can lead to increased memory consumption on long-running server processes. Only QUIC-enabled deployments are affected.

Impacted versions: <= v1.7.5

Resolution:

These issues have been addressed in s2n-tls version v1.7.6. We recommend upgrading to the latest version and ensuring any forked or derivative code is patched to incorporate the new fixes.

Workarounds:

For CVE-2026-16317 (Silent Drop of TLS 1.3 Encrypted Records), there is no workaround that fully mitigates this issue. Configuring s2n-tls to use only TLS 1.2 security policies would avoid the affected code path, but this is not recommended as it removes the security benefits of TLS 1.3.

For CVE-2026-16318 (QUIC Transport Parameters Memory Leak During HelloRetryRequest), deployments that do not enable QUIC are not affected and do not require any action. For QUIC-enabled deployments, restarting server processes periodically can reclaim the unreachable memory as a temporary mitigation.

References:

CVE-2026-16318

Bulletin ID: 2026-015-AWS
Scope: AWS
Content Type: Important
Publication Date: 04/7/2026 3:30 PM PST

Description:

Firecracker is an open source virtualization technology that is purpose-built for creating and managing secure, multi-tenant container and function-based services.

We identified CVE-2026-5747, an out-of-bounds write issue in the virtio PCI transport in Firecracker 1.13.0 through 1.14.3 and 1.15.0 on x86_64 and aarch64 that might allow a local guest user with root privileges to crash the Firecracker VMM process or potentially execute arbitrary code on the host via modification of virtio queue configuration registers after device activation. No AWS service is affected.

Impacted versions: Firecracker >= 1.13.0 AND <= 1.14.3 AND 1.15.0

Resolution:

This issue has been addressed in Firecracker version 1.14.4 and 1.15.1. We recommend upgrading to the latest version and ensuring any forked or derivative code is patched to incorporate the new fixes.

Workarounds
The virtio PCI transport is opt-in via the --enable-pci command-line flag when starting Firecracker. The legacy MMIO transport is the default and is not affected by this issue. Users who have enabled PCI transport can revert to MMIO by removing the --enable-pci flag from their Firecracker invocation. Note that switching from PCI to MMIO transport may result in reduced I/O throughput and increased latency.

Bulletin ID: 2026-043-AWS
Scope: AWS
Content Type: Important (requires attention)
Publication Date: 06/12/2026 11:45 AM PDT

Description:

AWS Common Runtime aws-c-http is a HTTP client library used by AWS SDKs for handling http requests to AWS services. We identified CVE-2026-12043, an issue where improper handling of HPACK dynamic table size updates in the AWS Common Runtime aws-c-http library might allow a remote actor operating a server to cause memory corruption on a connecting client application, potentially leading to arbitrary code execution, via a crafted sequence of HTTP/2 HEADERS frames.

Impacted versions: aws-c-http >= 0.4.22 AND <= 0.10.15

Exposed in following sdk versions:

aws-sdk-cpp >= 1.11.41, <= 1.11.814
aws-sdk-java-v2 >= 2.44.27, <= 2.44.14

Resolution:

This issue has been addressed in aws-c-http version 0.11.0. We recommend upgrading to the latest version and ensuring any forked or derivative code is patched to incorporate the new fixes.

Workarounds:

Force HTTP/1.1 connections if available.

CVE-2026-18394 - Incorrect authorization in Strands Agents Tools http_request tool

Bulletin ID: 2026-069-AWS
Scope: AWS
Content Type: Important (requires attention)
Publication Date: 07/31/2026 12:30 PM PDT

Description:

Strands Agents is an open-source SDK for building AI agents. The strands-agents-tools package provides pre-built tools for use with the SDK, including the http_request tool for making HTTP API requests.

We identified CVE-2026-18394, an incorrect authorization issue in the http_request tool. Operators can use the HTTP_REQUEST_TOKEN_CONFIG allowlist to bind a credential to a set of approved hostnames so it is sent only to those hosts. The tool also exposed a proxies parameter in the input schema that the large language model (LLM) could control. A crafted prompt, for example one delivered through untrusted web content the agent reads (indirect prompt injection), could set proxies to an actor-controlled endpoint. The hostname allowlist check still passes on the request URL, the credential is attached, and the request is routed through the actor's proxy on the first hop, disclosing the credential in cleartext in the Authorization header.

Impacted versions: < 0.8.2

Resolution:

This issue has been addressed in strands-agents-tools version 0.8.2. We recommend upgrading to the latest version and ensuring any forked or derivative code is patched to incorporate the new fixes. As a precautionary measure, we recommend all operators who configured credentials via HTTP_REQUEST_TOKEN_CONFIG on affected versions rotate those credentials, even if there is no indication a credential was exposed.

Workarounds:

Until you can upgrade, do not bind credentials with HTTP_REQUEST_TOKEN_CONFIG when the http_request tool is available to an agent that processes untrusted content, and configure any required proxies out of band through the HTTP_PROXY and HTTPS_PROXY environment variables rather than through the tool.

References:

GHSA-qhw6-2h72-m84v

19th October – Threat Intelligence Report

October 19, 2026

For the latest discoveries in cyber research for the week of 19th October, please download our Threat Intelligence Bulletin.
TOP ATTACKS AND BREACHES

CenterPoint Energy, a US utility company serving Texas and several other states, has disclosed a data breach affecting more than 1 million Texas residents. Unauthorized access to an external system exposed names, addresses, Social Security information, and driver’s license numbers, according to regulatory notifications filed by the company.
Burger King Japan, operator of the international fast-food chain in Japan, has disclosed a breach affecting approximately 11.18 million application members. Unauthorized access between October 2 and 7 exposed contact information, birth dates, gender, and regional details. The company found no evidence of compromised passwords or payment cards.
ConnectWise Cloud Backup, a Microsoft 365 backup service used by managed service providers, has suffered a credential compromise enabling unauthorized access to customer environments. Attackers used compromised application credentials to sign in to at least 173 organizations, potentially accessing email, files, and Teams information before access was suspended.
Several French supermarkets, including E. Leclerc stores, have experienced cyberattacks targeting connected refrigeration controllers. Attackers reportedly manipulated temperature settings, causing refrigeration system failures, food losses, and operational disruption. Losses from the attacks exceeded $100,000 for one retailer.

AI THREATS

Check Point researchers have identified critical vulnerabilities in LiteLLM, a widely used AI model gateway. CVE-2026-35029 and CVE-2026-59823 could allow low-privileged users to change configurations, access sensitive files, redirect requests, and steal credentials. Successful exploitation could enable administrative takeover or remote code execution. LiteLLM addressed both flaws.
Check Point researchers have demonstrated how peer influence can cause AI agents working in teams to violate established rules. In controlled experiments, repeated changes in teammate behavior increased one agent’s violation rate from 44% to 98%. The agents rarely acknowledged peer influence when explaining their decisions.
India’s national cybersecurity response team, CERT-In, has reported unauthorized access to organizational systems involving autonomous AI agents. The activity exploited exposed credentials, insecure application interfaces, and misconfigured cloud services to retrieve business information. Compromised credentials also enabled repeated access without detection by the affected organizations.

Microsoft has released its October 2026 Patch Tuesday updates, addressing a record 1,413 vulnerabilities across Windows, Office, SharePoint, and other products. The updates address several critical flaws and three zero-days. Among them is CVE-2026-96951, an actively exploited Windows Shell vulnerability that allows attackers to bypass security protections.

title: Compromised ConnectWise Cloud Backup identities used to access Microsoft 365 tenants
text:
October 19, 2026

|

Security intelligence

Compromised ConnectWise Cloud Backup identities used to access Microsoft 365 tenants

By Field Effect Security Intelligence Team

At a glance:

ConnectWise discovered unauthorized access involving application identities associated with ConnectWise Cloud Backup on October 14, disclosed the incident on October 16, and disabled affected application identities on October 17.

Field Effect notified affected clients on October 16, the same day of the disclosure, after identifying tenants that had authorized the affected ConnectWise Cloud Backup application.

Microsoft Threat Intelligence observed successful authentication activity using the compromised application identity across customer Microsoft 365 tenants, followed by Microsoft Graph reconnaissance and attempts to establish persistence.

Researchers confirmed that the compromised vendor credential was used to gain unauthorized access to customer Microsoft 365 environments and observed attempts to create additional trusted credentials inside affected tenants.

Threat summary
ConnectWise is investigating a security incident involving unauthorized access to application identities associated with ConnectWise Cloud Backup, formerly known as SkyKick.
The company disclosed the incident on October 16, 2026, and has since suspended Cloud Backup, SaaS Security, and Cloud Management services while containment, remediation, and forensic activities continue.
As of October 19, ConnectWise reported that it had not observed successful threat activity in environments it monitors after implementing containment measures, although the investigation remains active.
ConnectWise Cloud Backup integrates directly with Microsoft 365 to perform backup and recovery operations. To do this, customers grant the service permission to access resources such as Exchange Online, SharePoint, OneDrive, Teams, directory data, and Microsoft Graph, the application programming interface (API) used by Microsoft 365 services. Once approved, the application can authenticate directly to Microsoft cloud services and operate with the permissions assigned within each tenant.
Researchers confirmed that a credential used by ConnectWise Cloud Backup was compromised and used to obtain Microsoft Graph access tokens across customer tenants. Microsoft Graph was not compromised. Instead, the threat actor obtained a credential belonging to a trusted application that already had permission to use Microsoft Graph on behalf of customer organizations. Because Microsoft recognized the application as trusted, the threat actor was able to authenticate as the service itself and inherit the permissions already assigned to it.
Microsoft Threat Intelligence assessed that the threat actor abused permissions previously granted to the application, including high-privilege permissions such as Directory.ReadWrite.All. Microsoft observed successful service principal authentication, Microsoft Graph reconnaissance, and attempts to add additional credentials to service principals after access was obtained.
As part of its response, ConnectWise disabled or revoked access associated with seven Cloud Backup and Cloud Management integrations. These applications had been granted access to customer Microsoft 365 environments to perform backup, management, and recovery functions. Researchers later reported activity involving multiple Cloud Management applications in addition to ConnectWise Cloud Backup, indicating that the activity extended beyond a single application.
Researchers also observed activity designed to expand and maintain access after the initial compromise. In one tenant, a ConnectWise Cloud Management - MS Teams application assigned itself the Global Administrator role and added credentials to other trusted applications. Those credentials could then be used independently of the original ConnectWise credential, creating persistence that would survive credential rotation or revocation.

PLEX2SHELL EXPLOIT USED TO TURN VULNERABLE PLEX SERVERS INTO CRYPTO MINERS
Pierluigi Paganini

October 19, 2026
Attackers exploit Plex2Shell flaws to install crypto miners and proxy software. Admins should update their Plex Media Server.

Plex Media Server is designed to make movies, music, and other media available across devices. But when a server is exposed to the internet and runs vulnerable software, it can become an entry point for attackers who have little interest in your film collection.

On October 16, 2026, security researcher Zach Main published technical details and proof-of-concept (PoC) code for a vulnerability chain dubbed Plex2Shell. Within a day, researchers had observed attackers using the exploit against an internet-facing honeypot, deploying cryptocurrency-mining malware and proxy software. The incident is a reminder of how quickly a public exploit can be weaponized by threat actors.

The chain combines four vulnerabilities in Plex Media Server: CVE-2026-96652, CVE-2026-96654, CVE-2026-96655, and CVE-2026-96656. Together, they can allow attackers to execute arbitrary code on vulnerable servers without valid credentials, provided the required conditions are met. The code runs with the privileges of the Plex service, giving attackers an opportunity to install additional software and abuse the host.

The technical details are available in Main’s original analysis, Plex2Shell. Plex had been notified of the vulnerabilities on July 27 and acknowledged the report on August 4, awarding a bug bounty. The company released fixes in September, before the exploit code became public.

The loader does not check the library’s name, executable permissions, digital signature, or symbols. As a result, the library’s ELF constructor can run with the same privileges as the Plex service.

Meta wants to scrape your website to train its AI, and you can’t say no

Pierluigi Paganini
October 19, 2026

Meta wants the right to scrape your website for AI training. If you have a business account, that includes you.

At the end of the month, Meta plans to change its commercial terms in a way that matters to every company advertising or selling through its platforms. The new language takes effect on October 30, 2026. It lets Meta collect content from websites associated with business customers and use it to train AI models or otherwise improve its products, according to The Register.

Meta defines “business customer” broadly. It includes anyone who uses ads or marketing messages, sells or lists products, develops apps, uses a product catalog, manages a Page, runs a Group for business purposes, or uses tools such as Ads Manager or Meta Business Suite. At least one million businesses already use Meta’s AI agents in WhatsApp and Messenger. Nieman Lab also points out that almost every news publisher has at least one Meta business account.

The contract clearly explains which tools Meta can use. By accepting the terms, you allow Meta, or anyone working on its behalf, to use automated tools such as web scrapers, bots, spiders and crawlers to access and index your websites, pages and URLs. These tools can also revisit your sites regularly to collect updates.

“You authorise us (or any entity acting on our behalf) to use automated software (such as web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers and user agents) and create test credentials to access, index, cache, analyse, collect, retrieve or crawl the domains, web pages or URLs (and any content available through them) that are associated with your products or services, or that are made available through your or users’ use of Meta Company Products and services, and to periodically pull updates from such domains, web pages or URLs.” states Meta’s commercial terms. “Meta may use any content from such domains, web pages or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train and maintain the integrity of, the Meta Company Products, services and features provided under these Commercial Terms and any other applicable supplemental terms.”

Then comes the use clause. The company may use any content from those domains to provide, develop, improve, research, train and maintain the integrity of its products, services and features. The contract lists scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers and user agents, which is a lot of ways to say visitor you didn’t invite.

The News/Media Alliance says there’s no way out. Business accounts have no option to opt out of the terms, and the only alternative is to stop using Meta’s products.

““Meta’s new commercial terms of use are outrageous and probably illegal. The company’s decision to withhold access to its audience unless businesses allow Meta to scrape content from their websites is an appalling, bad-faith policy, and a clear abuse of the company’s market power. It cannot be allowed to be implemented on October 30.” states Media Alliance. “The text is so far reaching that any business with intellectual property online and a Meta business account could have their copyrighted material taken from them.”

Danielle Coffey, President and CEO of the News/Media Alliance also pushed the point beyond news sites. Her questions were whether Taylor Swift’s Meta business account would give Meta access to copyrighted media on her website, and whether Shutterstock’s would let Meta scrape its images. The Alliance’s argument is that any business with intellectual property online and a Meta account could be affected, not just publishers.

There is also a problem with robots.txt. Cybersecurity firm Calif published a full exploit and write-up this week for a local privilege escalation on OpenBSD 7.9 that chains two separate kernel flaws, one of them a 37-year-old integer overflow inherited from the original BSD sources. The exploit bypasses OpenBSD’s KARL address randomization and the SMAP and SMEP hardware protections without needing any information disclosure vulnerability at all.

OpenBSD already shipped patches for both issues in September: the integer overflow fix in errata 018 on September 14, and the related use-after-free fix in errata 026 on September 30. Both are available through syspatch and cover all architectures.

The shared memory attachment counter, shm_nattch, was defined as a signed 16-bit integer in BSD source code in 1988. It could hold a maximum value of 32,767. OpenBSD inherited this definition and never changed it. When the affected socket closes, the resulting counter updates modify page table entries, allowing user memory to be accessed with supervisor-level privileges. Log Analysis: From Raw Events to Detections
text:
An enterprise environment emits events by the million every hour. During an incident, the responder rarely needs all of them. They need the few hundred that tell the story: the burst of 4625 failures followed by a single 4624 success, the encoded PowerShell spawned by winword.exe, the new service installed at 03:12 on a domain controller. Logs analysis is the discipline of getting from the first number to the second fast enough to matter.

That job has become harder in two directions at once. Attackers using AI tooling generate evidence at machine speed and pad real actions with benign-looking activity. Meanwhile, the obvious shortcut of pushing logs into an LLM runs into guardrails, context-window limits and data-protection obligations. Hugging Face’s responders hit exactly that wall in July 2026, when roughly 17,000 events were refused by frontier models and had to be processed on a local model instead.

Below, we cover log analysis end to end, then look at LogTotal, SOC Prime’s free answer to the incident-time version of the problem.

What Are the Fundamentals of Log Analysis?

Every log analysis workflow, whether it runs in a SIEM, a data lake or a responder’s laptop, rests on the same five stages. Skipping one usually shows up later as a missed detection or a false positive nobody can explain.

Collection. Agents, syslog forwarders, API pollers and cloud-native exporters move events off the source. Gaps here are silent: a Sysmon config that drops Event ID 10 (process access) means credential-dumping via LSASS never appears downstream.

Parsing and normalization. Raw lines become fields. A source IP should be the same field whether it came from a firewall, an IdP or an EDR, which is why schemas like ECS and OCSF exist.

Enrichment. Asset criticality, user role, GeoIP and threat intelligence turn an IP address into context an analyst can act on.

Correlation. Single events rarely prove anything. Linking them by host, user, process GUID or session ID is what produces an attack narrative.

Retention and integrity. Hot storage for search, cold storage for forensics, and tamper evidence so the record holds up later.

What Is Log Analysis?

Log analysis is the process of examining machine-generated records to reconstruct what happened on a system, decide whether it matters, and determine what to do next. In security operations, it answers five questions about any suspicious activity: who acted, on what asset, when, from where, and by which mechanism.

It is distinct from log management. Management is plumbing: ingestion, storage, retention, access control. Analysis is interpretation. A team can have a well-run log pipeline and still miss an intrusion because nobody, human or machine, is asking the right questions of the data.

In practice, log analysis runs in three modes:

Detection. Rules and models evaluate events continuously and raise alerts when known malicious behavior appears.

Investigation. After an alert or a tip-off, analysts pivot through related events to scope the incident and find root cause.

Threat hunting. Analysts start from a hypothesis, such as abuse of a specific LOLBin, and search proactively for evidence the detection layer missed.

Of all the teams that use logs, security has the least room for gaps.

Why Is Log Analysis So Important?

Because time drives breach cost, and logs are where time is won or lost. IBM’s 2026 Cost of a Data Breach Report puts the mean time to identify and contain a breach at 247 days, the first increase in five years. Breaches with a lifecycle over 200 days averaged $5.65 million, against $4.32 million for those contained faster.

Beyond cost, log analysis underpins four obligations every security program carries:

Detection. EDR and NDR see slices of activity. Logs from identity providers, SaaS audit trails and cloud control planes fill the gaps between them.

text: Jump to sectionOVHcloud CLI supply chain compromise: release assets replaced through a GlassWorm-hijacked contributor accountOct 20, 2026 · @6mileSummaryOn 19 October 2026, between 12:47 and 13:12 UTC, an attacker replaced the release binaries of five already-published versions of OVHcloud’s official CLI (ovh/ovhcloud-cli, v0.11.0 to v0.15.0) with a secret-stealing build. The uploads were made through the GitHub account HassenBF, a legitimate OVH contributor, using the ordinary GitHub Releases API. No tag was pushed and no GitHub Actions workflow ran. The malicious binary was a go build from a workstation with uncommitted changes, dropped straight onto existing releases. A downstream user whose CI pinned a SHA-256 caught it within 94 minutes. OVHcloud deleted the files at 14:21 UTC and shipped a clean, immutable v0.16.0 about three hours later.The HassenBF account was already compromised and had been for seven months. Its public repositories show a scripted history rewrite on 5 March 2026 and a hidden preinstall.js loader that decodes to a second stage using a Solana memo dead drop. The wallet is a known GlassWorm indicator, and the amend-and-force-push technique matches the ForceMemo campaign. The earliest server-verified use of the account by the attacker is 5 March 2026, about 228 days before the asset replacement. Whether the same actor did both is our inference, and we cover its limits below.This is a release-asset replacement attack. The source repository was never touched, so anyone verifying against the Go module proxy or building from source was fine. But anyone who ran install.sh, brew install --cask ovh/tap/ovhcloud-cli, or downloaded a tarball from GitHub in that window on macOS, Linux x86_64/arm64 or Windows x86_64 got the malware.Scope and limitsWe built the timeline from server-side GitHub data (the repository Activity API, Actions run records and release records), not from git author, committer or tagger dates, which the pusher controls. OVHcloud deleted the replaced binaries before anyone archived them, so we have not analyzed the payload, and we could not independently confirm the 12:47 to 13:12 replacement times. Those come from the reporter’s capture in issue #300. The link between the March account compromise and the October asset replacement rests on the shared account identity, not on anything we observed directly. We found no PolinRider markers, no malicious workflow additions and no GhostAction indicators. The affected versions come from OVHcloud’s statements and the public issue, which lists v0.13.0 to v0.15.0. Release timestamps and the assets left behind show v0.11.0 and v0.12.0 were also touched.TimelineOVHcloud’s public statements use Paris time (UTC+2), so we converted everything to UTC. The Tel Aviv, Israel, customer identity and access management provider wants Thompson to move it from a human identity orchestration to building foundational agent trust infrastructure. Thompson said Transmit will expand beyond its core base of large financial enterprises into the mid-market by streamlining implementation and adopting self-service models.

Thompson spent more than five years at Socure, where he helped the Nevada identity and risk intelligence vendor grow the business by more than 500%. Thompson replaces Mickey Boodaei, who led the company since helping establish it in October 2014. He will remain involved as chairman of Transmit's board and involved day to day in implementing product strategy, while Thompson said he will take a larger role in shaping product strategy and setting priorities across the organization.
"I see us providing foundational infrastructure for organizations to have visibility of what traffic is human traffic versus agent traffic," Thompson said. "That's kind of basic. Even as basic as it seems, it's a lot harder in practice."
AI agents are actively executing tasks inside applications, and Thompson said the blanketed blocking policies in place at many financial institutions today are unsustainable long-term. Legitimate agent use cases are rapidly growing. AI agents are more iterative, adaptable, and persistent than humans, which Thompson said requires dedicated security controls and customized user journeys.
"This isn't a tomorrow problem," Thompson said. "This is a yesterday problem for organizations to figure out, and a lot of them recognize they're behind. So they need a partner that's not just marketing that they can do things. They need a partner with real tech that can come in and start helping them identify and solve this and secure this problem today."
Thompson said Transmit can differentiate human versus agent traffic, govern agent authorization, and enforce human-in-the-loop or human-on-the-loop verification during high-risk actions like initiating wire transfers or executing trades. He said Transmit possesses live, production-ready agent trust technology deployed at major financial institutions, separating them from competitors with market-only claims.
"The agent trust infrastructure that we're providing to organizations not only helps with the security controls and risk management within the application, but it also will help enforce the human in the loop and the human on the loop protocols for organizations to make sure that agents are authorized to do things by humans where necessary," Thompson said.

Image: Shutterstock/ISMG

A backup and recovery software's update logic was weaponized to push malware from attacker-controlled servers in short bursts of time, researchers found.See Also: When Recovery Is Tested for Real: Lessons From Cyberattacks and Outages

Without relying on any vulnerability, hackers compromised Aomei's update and notification systems used by its disaster recovery tool Backupper, and remote access service AnyViewer, and delivered malware in repeated, minutes-long intervals from April to July.

The threat actor, tracked as UNC7017 by Google, opportunistically targeted any system polling the update distribution servers, including those used by IT services, telecommunications, higher education and other sectors in more than 10 countries. The campaign represents a new approach to supply chain attacks that does not require compromising source code or software build pipelines.

"This is the first time that we have encountered a software supply chain compromise that was implemented with these very short windows, effectively evading traditional point-in-time triage and automated file scanning," said Tyler McLellan, principal threat analyst at Google Mandiant.

Google said it has notified affected organizations, and Aomei has taken steps to secure its distribution servers.

Aomei is a Hong Kong-based data backup and management software provider serving 190 million users across 180 countries. Its products are used by major companies such as Amazon, Microsoft, Cisco and Walmart.

Threat analysis lab ManageEngine initially discovered the malicious activity on May 28 when Aomei Backupper installed a modified version of commercial remote administration tool Radmin to establish persistent remote access on two unrelated endpoints from different countries in the same timeframe.

At that point, the threat actor had tampered with two configuration files used by Backupper and AnyViewer's built-in promotional content system.

One file, down_html.ini, tells the software where to download an update package and provides its version number and MD5 checksum, a unique fingerprint used to verify file integrity. The other file, Notifycfg.ini, tells the software's notification service what messages to display and which local programs to execute.

"The threat actor modified the update settings file on the update server to redirect the software to download a malicious ZIP package from attacker-controlled servers instead of legitimate updates," McLellan said. "The threat actor also altered the notification settings file on the update server to abuse the software's automatic notification service, forcing the system to immediately execute the downloaded malware locally."

"Neither configuration file is cryptographically authenticated by the client, and the checksum used to validate the archive is declared inside the same unauthenticated file that names it," said ManageEngine researchers Vishal Santharam, Praveen Kumar D and Veeramani Somasundaram.

Such diversions only lasted for five to 10 minutes each time before reverting configuration to authentic, clean content.

"Supply chain intrusions have historically focused on inserting backdoors into software source code or tampering with developer build pipelines," McLellan said. "UNC7017's use of ephemeral configuration tampering represents a lower-overhead, higher-stealth alternative."

The ZIP archive contains Crossroad, an initial downloader responsible for environment validation and staging secondary components. Crossroad checks for geolocation and whether multiple concurrent instances exist on the same host before proceeding to secondary downloads.

Image: Samuel Boivin/Shutterstock

Federal civilian agencies must remove DeepSeek from their networks.See Also: Securing AI Workloads With Ubuntu Pro
The U.S. Department of Homeland Security filed notice Monday of an order shutting the Chinese artificial intelligence developer out of civilian agency contracts and directing agencies to pull its products off their systems. The order comes more than a year and a half after the Navy, NASA and other agencies began blocking DeepSeek's chatbot on their own (see: DeepSeek Blocked In US Federal Agencies).
DHS warned that DeepSeek's models present "multiple threat vectors" and that agency use of them "could produce actionable intelligence on U.S. persons and/or government agencies."
"The models themselves may contain malware or other security vulnerabilities," the department said (see: Security Researchers Warn of New Risks in DeepSeek AI App).
Government employees or vendors using DeepSeek could additionally end up moving sensitive data to China, the department said. It also pointed to DeepSeek's servers in China, where it said Chinese law lets state cyber and intelligence services tap into privately held infrastructure.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin acted under the Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act of 2018, which grants the DHS secretary power to bar risky technology from civilian agency systems. The defense secretary and the director of national intelligence hold similar authorities to pull tech from military and intelligence networks. The Department of Defense invoked the law to blacklist Anthropic (see: Anthropic Seeks Full Appeals Court Review of Pentagon Ban).
The procurement ban applies to IT products and services from Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Co. and its affiliates. The removal mandate covers both the company's own offerings and third-party products and services "developed using DeepSeek implementations," likely including tools built on DeepSeek's open-weight models.
Mullin signed the order before Monday's notice. It urges agencies to watch network traffic for signs of data leaving their environments and to tighten logging.
The Federal Acquisition Security Council's implementing rule says exclusion and removal orders can reach prime contractors and subcontractors serving federal agencies. A 2023 Federal Acquisition Regulation update also requires contractors to follow exclusion and removal orders.
Texas has banned DeepSeek from state-issued devices since January 2025, and New York and Virginia followed within weeks. Australia, South Korea and Taiwan also keep it off government systems (see: Asian Governments Rush to Ban DeepSeek Over Privacy Concerns).
The House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party labeled DeepSeek a "profound threat" to national security in an April 2025 report that accused the app of sending American users' data to China. Lawmakers suggested DeepSeek likely leaned on distillation, training its model on outputs from U.S. AI systems (see: AI Firms Seek US Help Against China Model Distillation).
The order sets a 60-day window from its issuance for agencies to request exceptions, which the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency will approve or deny in writing. Under the 2018 law, a company targeted by an exclusion or removal order has 60 days after receiving notice to challenge it in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit.

title: Spend vs. debt: what's the bigger security risk?More cybersecurity spending doesn't mean better security. Organizations accumulate "security debt" through complexity & unnecessary controls, increasing fragility. Experts advocate for automation & tool integration over adding more layers. Real risk management measures resilience, not just compliance. CISOs must communicate cyber threats in business terms—revenue impact, recovery ability—to engage boards effectively. 🔒https://www.cio.com/article/4233353/spend-vs-debt-whats-the-bigger-security-risk.html#InfoSec #CyberSecurity
text:
by Carl Friedmann

Regional Executive Editor for EMEA

Spend vs. debt: what’s the bigger security risk?

Interview

Oct 14, 20266 mins

With a career built at companies like Visa, Ellie May, and Blackhawk, Selim Aissi, a 2026 CSO hall of fame inductee, understands how boards and executives demand a clear justification for cyber security investment, especially considering today’s difficult economic climate.But getting security leaders to communicate tech debt, operational fragility, and long-term cyber risk in business terms the board can actually act on isn’t always straightforward.

A lot of organizations add tools, and more platforms and controls in response to new threats. Yet that doesn’t necessarily address underlying complexities. Security investment can actually increase operational and strategic risk.

“I think there’s a tipping point once a reasonable depth of defense is in place,” he says. “When there’s a reasonable level of automation of security controls and cross integration of security tools, anything beyond that could potentially be overspend and could potentially add risk to the entire organization.”

So the challenge is to know when an environment exists and functions without the need for a sudden budget spike.

“All of the KRIs and KPIs in place should be able to indicate the level of resiliency,” he adds, “in addition to other controls such as making sure there are processes that would allow for detection of, let’s say, API abuse, cloud-level abuse, and, increasingly these days, AI as it adds yet another threat vector.”

Understanding risk also lies in recognizing the distinction between organizations that are genuinely resilient, and those that appear mature on paper, focused on fine-tuning policies, compliance, governance, and frameworks.

“These are all important but they shouldn’t be the main focus,” he says. “The first step is knowing where the data is and once in transit, how it needs to be protected with the most updated protocols.”

Aissi expands on how organizations unintentionally create risk through tool sprawl and operational complexity, how boards should think about long-term cyber resilience, and why AI and cloud expansion are accelerating security debt faster than many enterprises can manage. Watch the full video below for more insights, and be sure to subscribe to the monthly Center Stage newsletter by clicking here.

On resiliency: A security organization that’s mature — and I’ve seen many and have built several — is one that’s architecturally designed to be resilient. But resiliency means different things to different people. To me it means that recoverability is tested often, making sure that in case of an event or breach case of lateral movement, the company can react according to a very clear playbook that’s been thoroughly tested. I also think a resilient organization is one that has the right controls of the right places, and one that also has metrics around them that indicate if there’s an event, and how well the tools work.

An area which I’m really passionate about is data protection. But how do you know the data is protected? A resilient organization doesn’t look at whether the data is encrypted at rest or not. It looks at the entire lifecycle of that PII. Meaning the organization has a very clear discovery mechanism to know exactly where the data is. It could be on laptops, servers, or in a public cloud. It could be in many different places, and it can be structured or unstructured.

On organizational risk: My definition of security debt is the accumulation of risk because of investment in areas where complexity is added, where a lack of automation is exaggerated, and where there’s overcompensation for some controls that aren’t needed. So if an organization spends money without effectively simplifying security controls, and automating more than what needs to be automated, that is tech debt.

text:
Key takeaways

In Japan, Qilin is the ransomware group most people can name. It claimed the 2025 attack that stopped Asahi Group's orders and shipments for about two months, Japan's police counted it as the most common ransomware in 2025, a man believed to be one of its leaders was detained in Japan this year, and it has now listed the railway group Keio.
On the leak sites, 2026 looks different. According to the tracking site ransomware.live, The Gentlemen has listed 23 Japanese organizations so far this year, more than any other group. Qilin has listed 15. The Gentlemen had listed none before January.
The Gentlemen is not entirely new. Group-IB says it grew out of one of Qilin's most active affiliate teams, which broke away in a dispute over unpaid commission in 2025.
Japanese organizations on its list that have confirmed an attack include Medica Publishing, whose breach may have exposed about 772,000 records, the textile maker Omikenshi and Saga University.
In our view, Japan's current wave of data breach disclosures should not crowd out ransomware on the management agenda. A breach costs money and trust; ransomware can stop the business for weeks.
Its usual way in is the same one Japan's police keep reporting: VPN devices and firewalls, especially FortiGate, with stolen or weak credentials. In our view, that matters far more than which brand ends up on the ransom note.

Why Japan knows the name Qilin#
Few ransomware groups become household names. In Japan, Qilin did.

Asahi Group, September 2025. The brewer's order and shipment systems were down for about two months, one of the most disruptive attacks Japan has seen. Qilin claimed it, and Japan's information security agency IPA names it in connection with the attack in its 2026 white paper.
Police statistics. In the National Police Agency's figures for 2025, Qilin's share of cases "increased sharply". Of the cases where the ransomware could be identified, it accounted for the most, ahead of LockBit, as we set out in our guide to Japan's ransomware statistics.

text:
Exploitation confirmed - public proof-of-concept - CVE-2026-80344 is a high-severity server-side request forgery (SSRF) in Apache Camel 4.0.0 through 4.18.4 and 4.19.0 through 4.22.0 that lets a remote AS2 sender force the Camel instance to connect to a host of the attacker’s choosing. Fixed in Apache Camel 4.23.0, with backports in 4.18.5 and 4.22.1.
Overview
Apache Camel’s AS2 component handles the AS2 EDI messaging protocol used for business-to-business document exchange. When a partner requests an asynchronous Message Disposition Notification (MDN), the receiving Camel instance sends a receipt to an address the sender supplies. Before this fix, camel-as2 took that address directly from the inbound message and used it as the destination for the outgoing receipt, without checking it against anything the deployment had configured.
In short, the attacker controls where the server connects next.
Versions before 4.0.0 are not affected by this specific code path. The 4.18.x LTS stream is affected through 4.18.4, and the 4.22.x LTS stream through 4.22.0.
Impact
A remote, unauthenticated AS2 partner can direct the Camel instance to make outbound connections to any address it can reach. That includes hosts that are only routable from inside the deployment’s network, such as internal services, metadata endpoints, and admin interfaces that are normally shielded from the internet. The AS2 receiver becomes a pivot point.
Where the deployment has configured credentials for MDN delivery, those credentials are presented to the attacker-chosen destination. An attacker can therefore capture them or use them against legitimate targets. CVSS scores this at 8.2 (HIGH): network-reachable, low complexity, no privileges or user interaction required.
Remediation
Upgrade to Apache Camel 4.23.0, which fixes the issue. The asynchronous MDN destination is now constrained instead of taken verbatim from the inbound message.

Users on the 4.18.x LTS stream: upgrade to 4.18.5.
Users on the 4.22.x LTS stream: upgrade to 4.22.1.

If you cannot upgrade immediately:

Restrict outbound connectivity from the AS2 receiver so it can only reach the partner endpoints it legitimately delivers receipts to. Deny everything else, including link-local and internal RFC 1918 ranges the receiver has no reason to touch.
Do not attach credentials to MDN delivery that are valid for any host other than those partners.
Log and alert on outbound connections from the AS2 receiver that fall outside its expected destination set.

Security Insight
This is the same class of mistake that keeps recurring in integration middleware: trusting a value from the inbound message to decide where the server goes next. Apache has been unusually busy patching Camel this cycle, and the pattern in middleware frameworks is consistent - protocol handlers get built for interop first and bound-checked later. Compare the ActiveMQ CVE-2026-34197 situation, where an Apache messaging component also became the front door for attackers. Teams running B2B gateways should treat every SSRF fix as a reminder to audit their own egress allowlists, not just their patch level.

# 48 New Technology Sector Incidents Hit Wire as ConnectWise Supply Chain Attack Spreads

Tech took a beating this past week. It was the main target for attackers (ranking #2 out of 12 sectors) with 193 stories hitting the wire. Things didn't slow down today either, since we saw 48 new incidents in that sector alone. The volume is high, but it hides a shift in tradecraft that defenders usually miss because they're too busy hunting for zero-days.

Complex software exploits aren't really on the rise. Instead, attackers are using administrative access to turn security and management tools into delivery vehicles for compromise. It's what I call administrative leverage. They use the trusted relationship between a service provider and its clients to bypass the perimeter entirely.

The ConnectWise situation is the clearest example right now. The attackers didn't need some clever flaw in the backup software (which is odd, given how we usually think these things work). They just used compromised credentials to get into the cloud backup service and then jumped from there into the Microsoft 365 environments of various MSP partners and their clients. The provider became the bridge.

Then you have Rank Math PRO. Version 3.0.123 of that WordPress plugin was hit in a supply chain attack, sending out malware that allows for a full website takeover. It's the same principle applied to software distribution instead of service management. Once the plugin is trusted and installed, the attacker doesn't have to "break in." They're already inside the house because the user invited them.

The ETS breach follows a similar pattern of identity failure over technical wizardry. Some unauthorized party didn't use a sophisticated exploit to steal data from millions of California students; they just used compromised credentials to get into an SFTP server. It's a boring attack that gets massive results.

Industry folks like to treat these as separate incidents (one is a plugin, one is backup, one is SFTP). They aren't. These are all different ways of playing the same hand: target the entity that holds the keys for everyone else.

I have a moderate level of confidence that we're seeing a tactical pivot away from complex exploit chains toward this path of least resistance. To get my confidence to "high," I'd need more evidence that these credential thefts come from a coordinated effort to map MSP dependencies rather than just opportunistic scanning for leaked passwords.

It rhymes with the 2020 SolarWinds campaign in terms of the force-multiplier effect. In both cases, the attacker finds one point of failure and gets access to thousands of downstream targets. But the parallel breaks when you look at the "how." SolarWinds was a masterpiece of engineering (a stealthy build-process compromise requiring deep knowledge of software pipelines). Today's attacks are often just lazy. They don't need an elite lab; they just need a stolen session token or a password reused from another breach.

The problem is we've spent five years treating Managed Service Providers as security multipliers. The logic was simple: if you can't afford a top-tier SOC, pay an MSP who has one. But that ignores the fact that you aren't just outsourcing management; you're concentrating your risk. You're putting all your eggs in a basket managed by someone whose security posture you can't actually verify.

The most dangerous part isn't the immediate data loss. It's the second-order effect on downstream clients who might not even know they're exposed. If an MSP's credentials are gone, every one of their clients is effectively breached, regardless of how many firewalls they have installed. The attacker isn't fighting the firewall; they're using the administrator's key to open the door from the inside.

The 7 biggest issues CISOs and security teams face today

Feature

Oct 12, 202612 mins

Year after year CISOs see the volume, velocity, and sophistication of attacks increase. They also see their attack surfaces expand and increase in complexity.

Advances in artificial intelligence and the rapid growth of AI use in business are also impacting the security agenda, introducing novel attacks, broadening the attack surface to include AI infrastructure, and presenting governance and security control challenges and complications — especially as agentic systems come online.

As a result, 68% of security leaders report that their roles have become more stressful over the past five years, according to the 2026 State of Cybersecurity survey from ISACA, with 71% of CISOs citing the increasingly complex threat landscape as their main stressor, up from 63% in 2025.

Moreover, the introduction of Mythos-class AI models has 50% of CISOs considering exiting the profession entirely, according to a recent survey from Absolute.

To tackle this increasingly complex and intense security environment, security leaders must sharpen their strategies — and their teams’ skills — around the most pressing issues they and their CISO colleagues are facing today.

To help with that, we spoke with security chiefs and cyber experts to identify the seven biggest issues CISOs need to address, with insights on how to tackle the challenges.

1. Preventing compromise — with increased emphasis on resilience and recovery

Although CISOs are increasingly taking on governance responsibilities and business risk mandates, broadening their remit, Kyle McMillan, chief cybersecurity officer at Siemens USA, says all the work in the security organization is still “framed in the context of preventing a compromise.”

It’s a monumental task, McMillan says, as there’s no one formula for the right defense that will work for every CISO. Rather, CISOs must know the specific risk profile of their organizations, the specifics of their IT environment, and the general threat landscape, as well as any threats particular to their industry — and then use all that to formulate a unique plan of defense based on the resources available.

“And there are always trade-offs to be made,” McMillan adds.

While it’s true that thwarting attacks as much as possible and minimizing the damage in the event of a successful breach has always been job No. 1 for CISOs, research shows it’s one they continue to struggle with. The State of Incident Response Readiness, a 2026 report from incident response company Sygnia, found that 73% of CISOs weren’t fully ready for a major cyberattack.

That — and the rise of AI-assisted attack volumes and speed — is contributing to a mindset shift from prevention to resilience. Yes, prevention remains job No. 1, but ensuring business continuity and resilience in the event of an incident is becoming a key emphasis and addition to CISOs’ playbooks. That means honing incident response plans, conducting more relevant tabletop exercises, and sharpening team operations to accelerate cyber recovery.

According to Foundry’s forthcoming Security Priorities Study, 69% of security leaders are currently undertaking this shift.

One of the biggest issues CISOs continue to face is accurately assessing their organization’s processes, infrastructure, and risk profile and then building a program tailored to their unique security requirements, says Ira Winkler, veteran cybersecurity leader and now CEO and program director of CruiseCon, which offers professional education for security leaders.
