“We are working urgently to establish the extent of the damage and determine the cause, and will implement the necessary measures to strengthen security,” Nikkei stated.

The breach in numbers
Nikkei Inc. disclosed a cybersecurity incident that exposed 1.83 million personal information records after attackers gained access to one of its systems. The company said most of the records contained no identifying information; specifically, 1.68 million records had no identifiers. About 150,000 records contained at least one of the following: full names, email addresses, physical addresses, telephone numbers, or dates of birth. Email addresses appeared in roughly 120,000 of the records. Nikkei also reported that no credit card information was exposed.

How the intruders got in
According to Nikkei’s notice, the intrusion occurred during the early morning hours of October 7. Hackers used stolen credentials to access a development system within Nikkei’s network. That unauthorized access exposed personal information the company stored in the cloud. Nikkei said it revoked the abused credentials and notified Japan’s Personal Information Protection Commission on October 11.

Burger King Japan (BK Japan) has announced a significant data breach involving the member information system of its official mobile application. Unauthorized third-party access resulted in the exposure of approximately 11.18 million member records. The compromised data includes a wide range of personally identifiable information (PII), creating a substantial risk of phishing and other social engineering attacks against the affected customers. The company has confirmed that financial information was not part of the breach and has notified the relevant Japanese data protection authorities.

Threat Overview
The breach occurred due to an unauthorized third party gaining access to Burger King Japan's systems between October 2 and October 7, 2026. The data leak was subsequently confirmed by the company on October 13. The attackers successfully accessed and potentially exfiltrated a database containing detailed information on members of the Burger King mobile app loyalty program. The specific method of access has not been disclosed, but it likely involved an exploited vulnerability in the application's backend infrastructure or compromised credentials.

Technical Analysis
The investigation into the root cause is ongoing, but the scope of the exposed data has been defined. The breach affected a database containing the following PII for 11.18 million users:

Member ID
Full Name (in Kanji and Kana)
Email Address
Date of Birth
Phone Number
Gender
Prefecture (region in Japan)
Mobile ordering usage status
Email verification status

Burger King Japan has stated that it does not store credit card numbers in this system, which significantly mitigates the risk of direct financial fraud. The status of login passwords was not confirmed as leaked, but this remains under investigation. The combination of the other data points, however, is highly valuable for attackers.

Impact Assessment
While no financial data was lost, the exposure of 11.18 million detailed personal records presents a major security risk. Attackers can use this information to conduct highly convincing and targeted phishing campaigns. For example, an attacker could send an email to a victim that addresses them by their full name and references their date of birth or location, tricking them into revealing more sensitive information like passwords or financial details.
For Burger King Japan, this incident will result in significant reputational damage and loss of customer trust. The company will also face scrutiny from Japan's Personal Information Protection Commission and may be subject to penalties. The cost of incident response, investigation, and customer notification will also be substantial.

The hacker known as ChimeraZ claimed responsibility. The exposed data includes nearly 118,000 unique email addresses, names, contact information, and specific details about their stays, creating a significant risk of follow-on phishing attacks.

The breach occurred in May 2026 but was just recently added to the HIBP database, bringing renewed attention to the incident. The attacker, ChimeraZ, who has been linked to other attacks on French tourism companies, successfully compromised Gîtes de France's systems and exfiltrated a customer database.

117,574 unique email addresses

The specific vector for the breach has not been publicly disclosed by Gîtes de France. However, the attacker, ChimeraZ, is known for exploiting common web application vulnerabilities.

Initial Access: The breach likely originated from an exploit against a public-facing web application (T1190), such as an unpatched vulnerability in the booking system's content management system (CMS) or a framework component.

The claim appeared on the group's data leak site on October 19, 2026. Helix alleges to have breached the company's network, exfiltrated data, and has threatened to publish the stolen information. American Campus, a company with approximately $1 billion in annual revenue, has not yet publicly commented on the alleged attack. This incident is part of a high-tempo campaign by the Helix group, which utilizes double extortion tactics to pressure victims into paying a ransom.
Threat Overview
On October 19, 2026, the Helix ransomware operation added American Campus to their list of victims. The group's typical modus operandi involves gaining initial access to a network, moving laterally to compromise key systems like domain controllers and file servers, exfiltrating large volumes of sensitive data, and finally, deploying their ransomware to encrypt systems. The public post on their leak site initiates the pressure campaign, threatening to release the stolen data if the ransom is not paid. Initial Access: Ransomware groups like Helix often gain entry through common vectors such as exploiting unpatched vulnerabilities in public-facing services (T1190), phishing campaigns (T1566), or purchasing access from initial access brokers.

Impact: Finally, the Helix ransomware payload is executed across the network, encrypting files and rendering systems unusable (T1486). A ransom note is left behind with instructions for payment.

The potential impact on American Campus is severe. A successful ransomware attack could lead to widespread operational disruption, affecting everything from property management systems to resident services and corporate operations. On October 17, 2026, OpenCode, a popular open-source AI coding agent from Anomaly Innovations, revealed a security breach impacting its Console product. An attacker gained unauthorized access to a legacy system, exposing API keys that users had stored for third-party AI services, including OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google. The breach affected approximately 1.4% of Console users, some of whom subsequently reported large, fraudulent charges on their AI provider accounts. OpenCode has termed this a "large scale distillation attack" and is working with the AI providers to address the incident. All affected users have been notified and urged to rotate their exposed API keys immediately.
Threat Overview
The breach stemmed from an attacker compromising a legacy OpenCode system that was slated for decommissioning. This system contained sensitive user data, including API keys for powerful AI models that users had linked to their OpenCode Console workspace. The "bring-your-own-key" (BYOK) model, while popular for its flexibility, concentrated significant risk in this single point of failure.
Upon gaining access to these keys, the attackers immediately began using them to make a high volume of requests to the AI service providers. This activity, dubbed a "distillation attack," involves using powerful, expensive models (like GPT-4 or Claude 3) to generate vast amounts of high-quality data. This data is then likely used to train a smaller, less capable, and cheaper-to-run model, effectively "distilling" the knowledge of the larger model at the victims' expense.
Technical Analysis
The attack highlights a critical vulnerability in the ecosystem of AI-powered developer tools. The primary TTPs are:

Exploit Public-Facing Application (T1190): The attacker gained initial access by exploiting an unspecified vulnerability in a legacy OpenCode system.
Steal Application Access Token (T1528): The core of the attack was the theft of API keys, which function as access tokens for the AI services. These keys were likely stored insecurely on the compromised legacy system.
Resource Hijacking (T1496): The attackers used the stolen keys to consume the victims' AI service credits for their own purposes (the distillation attack), leading to direct financial loss for the legitimate key owners.

This incident demonstrates that in the AI era, credentials are not just for data access but also for accessing expensive computational resources, creating a new motive for credential theft.
Impact Assessment
The immediate impact on the 1.4% of affected users was financial. Reports on social media showed users facing fraudulent bills ranging from hundreds to over $1,700. This direct financial loss is a tangible consequence of the breach. Beyond the financial cost, the incident damages trust in OpenCode and the broader ecosystem of AI developer tools that rely on the BYOK model. It forces a re-evaluation of the security responsibilities in such systems, where a vulnerability in one tool can have direct financial repercussions across multiple other services. For the AI providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google), this incident creates customer support challenges and potential revenue loss from chargebacks.

2026-10-19

# Burger King Japan Exposes 11.18 Million Customer Records via Smartphone App

Stop thinking about security as walls. You've already lost if you do. A high wall means nothing when you prop the back door open with a brick for the delivery guy.

That's what happened at Burger King Japan. They confirmed a breach that leaked 11.18 million customer records. Juniors see a statistic. I see a blast radius that should've been contained years ago.

Getting hit isn't the crime. I've cleaned up breaches since Code Red kept us awake. Attackers find a way in. That's just how it is. The real failure, the kind that gets a CISO fired, is why so much data sat at a single point of failure.

The attackers didn't use magic. When an app leaks 11 million records, it's usually an unsecured S3 bucket or a broken API endpoint allowing ID enumeration. An attacker asks for record one, then two, then three. The server keeps saying yes until the database is gone. It isn't fancy. A teenager could write the script in an afternoon.

Read the official statements. They use phrases like unauthorized access. They might call it sophisticated to make themselves look like victims of a state operation instead of their own laziness. They won't explain why 11 million records were available for bulk export. Why wasn't data encrypted at rest? Why was there no rate-limiting on the API to stop someone from grabbing a million records in ten minutes?

They avoid the word hoarding. But that is exactly what this is. Why does a burger app keep 11.18 million records in a hot, accessible state? If you don't need data for a live transaction, it doesn't belong on a server connected to the public internet.

What would this cost you on a Tuesday?

If you’re the one managing the fallout, it’s not just the regulatory fines or the legal fees. It’s the sheer logistical nightmare of notifying 11 million people that their data is gone. The cost isn't in the breach; it's in the cleanup. You have to pay for credit monitoring, you have to handle the PR disaster, and you have to explain to a board of directors why your "enterprise-grade" app acted like a public folder.

I’ve seen this movie before. NotPetya was different—that was a scorched-earth campaign designed to destroy—but the aftermath was similar in one way: the companies that survived weren't the ones with the best firewalls. They were the ones who had clean backups and a limited blast radius. Burger King Japan didn't have a limit. They had a wide-open field.

Some of you will argue that in a modern app ecosystem, you need high availability for customer data to provide a seamless user experience. You’ll say that encrypting everything or partitioning databases creates too much latency.

That is a convenient lie.

Speed doesn't mean you have to let one API key drain your entire customer list. It isn't some technical wall they hit. It's a choice. They chose convenience over containment and that is why they're in my column on a Monday afternoon.

The second-order effects are what actually worry me. Forget the lost records for a second. Think about what those records become. Those 11 million entries aren't rows in a SQL table; they're blueprints for phishing. An attacker doesn't just put these on a forum. They use them to build perfect lures. Imagine getting an email saying your Burger King Japan loyalty points expired and you should click here to claim them. When the lure fits the victim's habits, the click-through rate jumps. Now a data leak in a burger app has turned into credential harvesting for banking apps and corporate emails.

It isn't just the burger joint. Look at the news this week. iRhythm hit 8.2 million people. Daiichi Kosho lost over 8.7 million records. Hollys leaked just under 2.76 million pieces of info. These are massive, clumsy data dumps.

A security breach affecting open-source AI agent framework provider OpenCode could expose API keys linked to users of Anthropic, OpenAI and Google AI models.

On October 17, OpenCode confirmed a security breach that occurred the night before and affected its Console service, which allows teams to share access to AI models through centrally managed API credentials.

Rather than exposing the underlying OpenAI, Anthropic or Google keys to individual team members, Console stores each workspace’s credentials and uses them to authenticate requests to the respective providers.

OpenCode is a widely used AI agent platform designed for software developers. It has 217 stars on GitHub.

In a July 2026 interview with Y Combinator – financial backer of Anomaly, the company which develops and maintains OpenCode – the founder and CEO Jay V claimed OpenCode had reached approximately 13 million monthly active users and 4.6 million weekly active users.

OpenCode Points to Unauthorized Access to Legacy System

The incident was “related to a large-scale distillation attack that impacted 1.4% of OpenCode Console users,” said OpenCode on social media.

“We have notified them all this morning via email. If you did not get an email you were not impacted, it was a subset of users who had external providers linked,” the company added.

The email was made public by several OpenCode users on the dedicated subreddit forum and the official Discord channel.

The email said OpenCode had "identified unauthorized access to a legacy system that we were in the process of decommissioning" and that "third party provider keys (e.g. OpenAI, Anthropic) saved in your workspace may have been exposed."

Specifically, Dax Raad, one of the main contributors to OpenCode and co-founder of Anomaly, noted on X that the breach involved only "the OpenCode Console, not OpenCode itself.”

OpenCode also notified Anthropic, OpenAI and Google to remediate the issue.

Recommended Steps to Mitigate OpenCode Threat

In an incident response report, software supply chain security firm Safeguard provided recommendations for OpenCode users to identify whether they have been affected by the incident and mitigate its impact:

Key steps include:

Checking whether you may be affected: search your inbox for the subject line “Action Required: Potential provider key breach.” If you have received the email, follow the guidance provided. If not, still review your keys as a precaution

Identifying all potentially exposed keys: list every OpenAI, Anthropic and Google Gemini API key that was ever stored in an OpenCode Console workspace, including keys added by other workspace admins

Reviewing API usage for suspicious activity: check each provider’s usage and billing reports from 16 October onward, and further back if possible. Look for unexpected usage spikes, unfamiliar models or unexplained charges

Creating replacement keys: generate new API keys for any potentially exposed credentials before revoking the old ones. Use project- or workspace-specific keys with appropriate restrictions and spending limits

Revoking potentially exposed keys: disable or delete the old keys through the relevant provider dashboard. Do not assume a key is safe simply because it has not shown suspicious usage

Verifying that old keys no longer function: test revoked keys against the relevant provider APIs and confirm they return an authentication error rather than a successful response

« Le premier problème de la défense européenne n’est pas un problème d’argent mais de cohérence. Or la cohérence, contrairement à un budget, ne peut pas être votée tous les ans. (…) si l’Europe veut être capable de se défendre en 2050, elle ne doit pas uniquement y consacrer un budget hors norme, mais aussi aligner sa recherche, son équipement, ses ressources humaines, sa doctrine et sa volonté stratégique de façon à former un tout cohérent et crédible. (…) Les budgets de la défense européenne ont beau augmenter dans tous les pays, ils ne donneront lieu qu’à des capacités fragmentées et des chaînes de production qui feront double emploi, le tout sans vision politique coordonnée.».

De fait, la capacité d’une entité politique à se défendre dépend d’abord et avant tout de la cohérence militaire de ses forces, laquelle ne dépend qu’en partie de ses « capacités militaires » au sens propre (les équipements), mais aussi de leurs performances, de leur quantité, de la capacité de l’industrie à les renouveler après le premier choc, de l’entrainement et de la discipline de ceux qui les opèrent, de la façon dont ils sont utilisés, de la stratégie déployée par ceux qui les commandent, de la capacité de cette entité à les transporter sur le champ de bataille (à supposer qu’on puisse encore parler de « front » et « d’arrière » dans la guerre qui se déroule sous nos yeux) et encore d’une multitude d’autres facteurs que n’enferme que partiellement l’acronyme DORESE utilisé dans les armées françaises (Doctrine, Organisation, Ressources humaines, Equipement , Soutien des forces,  Entraînement) et son équivalent à l’OTAN : DOTMLPF-I. (Doctrine- Organization – Training – Materiel – Leadership and education – Personnel – Facilities – Interoperability).

Une telle cohérence militaire s’établit dans le temps long par la répétition de deux types d’exercices.

title: L’Allemagne éteindra-t-elle les feux de forêt en France ?
text:
L’Allemagne éteindra-t-elle les feux de forêt en France ?

Par Julien Fischer
La formule est volontairement provocatrice mais elle désigne un risque stratégique, celui de voir l’Allemagne devenir, par la combinaison de capacités lourdes, de technologies de détection et d’une politique d’influence européenne, un acteur structurant de la sécurité civile méditerranéenne. La France perdrait son rôle de leader européen dans les moyens de lutte et resterait principalement organisée autour de ses moyens historiques. Dans la bataille européenne contre les feux de forêt, l’enjeu n’est plus seulement de disposer d’avions bombardiers d’eau. Il est de maîtriser une chaîne de valeur complète composée de l’anticipation climatique, de renseignement territorial, de détection précoce, d’un système de commandement des opérations, de moyens aériens et terrestres, de données satellitaires, de normes d’interopérabilité et d’un marché industriel structuré. Sur cette chaîne de valeur, l’Allemagne construit progressivement des positions d’influence depuis quelques années qu’il serait imprudent de sous-estimer.
Une puissance qui équipe sa projection
L’acquisition par l’Allemagne de 60 hélicoptères lourds CH-47F Block II Chinook auprès de Boeing constitue d’abord un programme de défense. Il vise à remplacer les vieillissants CH-53G de la Bundeswehr. Le programme, d’environ 6,98 milliards d’euros, comprend les appareils, les pièces de rechange, la formation, les infrastructures et le soutien logistique. Les premières entrées en service sont prévues dès 2027. Il serait néanmoins réducteur d’analyser cette commande sous le seul angle militaire. En effet, ce type d’hélicoptère de transport lourd se transforme facilement en bombardier d’eau. Il apporte des capacités intéressantes dans la réponse aux catastrophes : transport rapide de personnels, acheminement de matériels, évacuation sanitaire, logistique dans les zones isolées, déploiement de moyens de commandement et, selon les configurations et équipements, appui aux opérations de lutte contre les incendies.
La question stratégique n’est donc pas de savoir si les 60 Chinook allemands viendront écoper sur les lacs provençaux. Elle est de comprendre que Berlin se dote d’une masse critique de mobilité lourde projetable, interopérable avec les alliés de l’OTAN et mobilisable dans des opérations de sécurité civile, de gestion de crise ou d’assistance européenne. Cette capacité peut être utilisée dans le Sud de l’Europe, là où les feux, sécheresses, canicules et tensions sur les infrastructures deviennent des facteurs de sécurité collective. À l’heure où l’Union européenne organise des solidarités opérationnelles via le mécanisme de protection civile et la réserve rescEU, celui qui possède les moyens disponibles, projetables et soutenables pèse mécaniquement sur les décisions. De plus, les engagements opérationnels sont directement financés par l’UE, ce qui dote l’armée allemande d’une capacité d’amortissement financière supplémentaire pour compenser les coûts supplémentaires à cette acquisition. L’Allemagne ne se dote donc pas seulement de capacités aériennes. Elle acquiert une capacité de présence, de soutien et surtout d’influence dans les crises européennes à venir.
Du feu visible au renseignement précoce
La deuxième dimension, plus décisive encore, se situe en amont de l’incendie, la détection. Dans une logique de sécurité civile moderne, la valeur ne réside pas uniquement dans la vitesse d’intervention après le départ de feu. Elle réside dans la capacité à repérer un signal faible avant qu’il ne devienne un sinistre majeur. C’est sur ce segment que des entreprises allemandes occupent déjà une position significative au niveau européen. Dryad Networks, entreprise allemande spécialisée dans la détection ultra-précoce, (soutenue par la France alors qu’elle est dotée d’entreprise avec les mêmes capacités) développe notamment le réseau Silvanet. The threat actor behind the GhostAction supply chain attack has expanded beyond injecting malicious GitHub Actions workflows into compromised projects to phish open-source developers and deliver a stealer malware disguised within a fake font file.

The latest evolution, detailed by OpenSourceMalware, signals that the attackers are actively refining their modus operandi in response to steps taken by GitHub to prevent the workflow from running.

According to the threat intelligence platform, the threat actor registered the domain "my-github[.]com" and pointed it at "193.32.204[.]199," the same IP address that's used as an exfiltration endpoint for data harvested from running the malicious workflow.

The domain was registered on October 9, 2026, 17 days after "my-gitlab[.]com" was registered. It's unclear if the latter code-hosting-themed domain is operated by the same threat actor.

"It follows the same my-<code-host>.com naming pattern, making it a useful pivot, but current infrastructure does not directly connect it to GhostAction," security researcher Paul McCarty said. "They use different registrars, registrant records, Cloudflare nameserver pairs, IP addresses, ASNs, and DNS designs, and no shared certificate or account artifact has been recovered."

Since then, the "my-github[.]com" domain has been used in a phishing email impersonating a GitHub security alert to target an open-source maintainer the same day it was registered. The message, sent from "noreply@my-github[.]com," warned of a new login to their GitHub account from Moscow, Russia, and instructed them to click on a link to secure their account.

The deceptive page, per OpenSourceMalware, is said to have acted as a reverse proxy, harvesting the victim's password and two-factor authentication (2FA) code, and injected JavaScript that authorized an OAuth app with permissions to modify their workflows so as to facilitate a GhostAction-style attack.

The fake login page also includes JavaScript to silently authorize a GitHub OAuth device flow with repo, workflow, and read:org scopes, granting it broad permissions to read/write repositories, modify Actions workflow files, and gain visibility into organization membership and related organizational data.

The idea is the same as device code phishing, where the end goal is to obtain an access token from GitHub and exfiltrate it to "my-github[.]com" on TCP/8443.

"The script receives a device code and user code, loads /login/device, extracts GitHub's forms from the returned HTML, and submits them automatically," McCarty explained. "It inserts the user code, locates an authorization form, adds authorize=1, and posts the approval through the victim's authenticated proxied session."

"The victim does not need to type the device code or consciously approve the OAuth application. This kit goes further by automating the user-code and authorization steps through the reverse-proxied session."

By stealing a repository-scoped OAuth token, it gives the attacker a reusable API credential. Furthermore, the permissions granted through the stealthy OAuth authorization are consistent with GhostAction's ability to enumerate repositories and inject malicious workflow files under ".github/workflows/."

"The actor can now combine repository-scale automation with individual social engineering against people whose accounts provide access to projects, organizations, registries, and downstream users," OpenSourceMalware said.

Threat actors began targeting Plex2Shell, a chain of four Plex Media Server vulnerabilities, one day after technical details and a working exploit went public.

The researcher who found the Plex2Shell bugs released a write-up and proof-of-concept (PoC) code on October 16. Tracked as CVE-2026-96652, CVE-2026-96654, CVE-2026-96655 and CVE-2026-96656, the flaws can be combined to run arbitrary code on an exposed server without valid credentials. The code runs with the same privileges as the Plex service.

The issues were reported to Plex on July 27, and the company confirmed them and awarded a bug bounty on August 4. On September 1, Plex announced it had already shipped fixes and asked server owners to upgrade.

A different researcher caught the attacks by setting up an internet-facing Plex honeypot running a vulnerable release. Before October 17, the decoy had drawn largely reconnaissance scans and generic attack attempts.

“As of this morning (Oct 17th), I finally saw in the wild exploitation,” the researcher wrote. The attackers used the publicly released exploit, the researcher said, though they may have tweaked the code.

The attackers were observed dropping a cryptocurrency miner built on XMRig. Later that day, a second program called myawesomeproxy also appeared on the honeypot. The researcher identified it as proxy software, and it shows a notice saying that anyone running it agrees to the potential use of their internet traffic.

“Plex may be hosted on residential IP and I think threat actors would love to have residential IP proxy to access corporate VPNs and emails,” the researcher wrote.

The researcher cautioned that the published indicators of compromise cover only activity seen on the honeypot.

In its September advisory, Plex recommended that all server owners install the newest release without delay.

Half the AI bot traffic hammering your website comes from Meta

AI agent traffic across DataDome’s network grew 41.5% quarter over quarter to nearly 25 billion requests in Q3 2026, according to the company’s AI Traffic Report Q3 2026. Meta’s Muse generated 29.1 million requests between September 22 and October 3, its first 12 days of full availability. In a sample of Muse traffic, 99.3% of requests came from cloud and CDN infrastructure.
Nearly half of the AI agent traffic recorded in 2026 through September occurred in Q3. The growth had left capacity plans and bot-management policies based on the previous quarter’s averages out of date.
Meta leads AI agent traffic
Meta-ExternalAgent and Meta-WebIndexer generated a combined 12.4 billion requests in Q3, accounting for 49.7% of AI agent traffic recorded. Meta-WebIndexer overtook Meta-ExternalAgent in September, which is interpreted as a sign of continued investment in AI answer generation. ClaudeBot ranked fourth for the quarter, overtaking GPTBot.

Top AI agents per month (Source: DataDome)

OpenAI, Anthropic and Amazon each use separate bots to collect training data, index pages for AI search and retrieve pages when users ask questions. Each bot has a distinct name, allowing website owners to allow or block it individually. These controls do not cover AI agents that browse websites through a regular browser without using those bot names.
This separation gives publishers a way to refuse model training while remaining accessible to AI search and answer services. It also helps AI companies develop search results with current information and source links, reducing their reliance on Bing, Google or Brave.
Each additional bot gives publishers another access setting to manage. Companies do not always explain upfront how each bot treats robots.txt, the file website owners use to communicate rules for automated access.
Agentic browser traffic nearly quintuples
Agentic browser traffic in the dataset rose from 12.5 million requests in August to 58.2 million in September. Excluding Muse, traffic more than tripled to 38.7 million requests.
ChatGPT’s cloud browser generated the most traffic in the category in September. Muse accounted for 33% of that month’s total after becoming fully available on September 22. Comet’s traffic fell 65% from July to September.
Muse is a personal AI agent that operates inside a dedicated cloud virtual machine containing a browser. DataDome includes it in the agentic browser category because its traffic is browser-driven.
Its daily traffic patterns were consistent with user activity instead of a scheduled crawl. In the sample, 8.9% of requests reached sensitive website endpoints, including login, payment, account creation, shopping cart and form pages. Forms accounted for 81% of that sensitive traffic, receiving about eight times as many requests as login pages.
“Muse is the first mass-market example of where agentic traffic is heading. It works from its own cloud virtual machine, so nearly all of its requests look like data-center traffic rather than a user’s device, and a meaningful share lands on forms and checkout flows,” said Jerome Segura, VP of Threat Research at DataDome.
“Policies that trust residential or ISP-based traffic won’t catch agents like this. Organizations need to validate agent identity, understand intent, and decide deliberately which agents to allow and what they’re authorized to do.”

Ransomware pressure now reaches employees’ homes and families

Ransomware attackers threatened employees’ family members or friends at 37% of organizations surveyed for Semperis’ 2026 Ransomware Risk Report. The survey covered 1,200 IT and security professionals at organizations that had experienced at least one successful ransomware attack.
“Ransomware has proven to be a great cash-generating activity for criminal syndicates, which have no hesitation about inflicting both cyber and physical harm,” said Mickey Bresman, Semperis CEO.
Threats reach beyond the workplace
Respondents described threatening messages, stalking and threats of physical harm. Criminals use these tactics to increase pressure on employees and their employers to meet ransom demands.
A quarter said employees or their family members needed medical or psychological treatment because of ransomware threats. Meanwhile, 23% reported swatting, where someone makes a false emergency report to send police to a person’s location.
Doxxing, which involves exposing someone’s personal information online without consent, was another consequence described by respondents. Some employees needed security protection or changed jobs, offices or homes following an attack.

What threats did attackers leverage? (Source: Semperis)

Documenting response roles across the organization and including procedures for threats against people outside the workplace, such as employees’ family members is recommended. Establishing relationships with law enforcement before an incident is also advised.
The personal consequences add to the pressure on staff responding to an attack.
“IT and cybersecurity staff are already dealing with high levels of stress,” says Tim Beasley, Semperis Senior Incident Response Consultant. “A ransomware attack takes that to a whole new level. I’ve seen CISOs literally say, ‘I’m out, I’m done, I can’t do this. It isn’t worth it.’ I’ve seen people walk out the door because leadership thought they mismanaged something that caused the breach to occur. It all takes a mental toll.”
Restoring operations can leave attackers with access
Some 69% of surveyed organizations experienced multiple successful ransomware attacks within the previous year.
Recovering from an incident requires teams to find how criminals entered, remove their access and check the systems being restored. Malware, backdoors and compromised accounts can give intruders a way back into the organization.
Pressure to resume operations can lead businesses to restore services before establishing whether attackers have been removed. That leaves unresolved weaknesses available for another intrusion.
Ransom payments remained common, with 59% of respondents saying their organization paid. Reasons included protecting customer information, limiting disruption and containing reputational damage. Some paid because they could not remove attackers from their environment.

A flaw in Broadcom's Wi-Fi setup software lets an attacker within radio range run code as root on Broadcom-based routers, without the network password or any pairing step, security researcher Quentin Kaiser disclosed on October 16.

He showed the attack working against home gateways supplied by three Belgian internet providers, in one case reading the Wi-Fi password off the device and in another opening a remote shell over the air. No CVE has been assigned to the flaw, and no fix has been deployed to the affected routers, Kaiser says.

The flaw is in Broadcom's version of Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS), the feature that lets a device join a Wi-Fi network without the password being typed in. Broadcom's code mishandles the reassembly of fragmented WPS setup messages, so an attacker in range can send crafted messages that corrupt the router's memory. From there, Kaiser built two things: a way to read memory back off the device, and a way to run his own code on it.

Against an Orange Belgium gateway, the Askey TCG3000 read the Wi-Fi password (the PSK) from the router's stored settings, sent it back over the air, and then joined the network with it.

Against a Proximus gateway, the Sagemcom-built BBOX3V+, the exploit opened a reverse shell, a remote command line, carried over Wi-Fi frames, so no outside server was needed.

Both ran without any login, and the attack works at a distance, not only up close, Kaiser says. He reports no real-world attacks using the flaw. The working exploits are his own.

What's Affected

Broadcom's WPS code is embedded in routers and access points from dozens of vendors, and Kaiser estimates that millions of devices worldwide are affected.

The vulnerable chips fall into two families: older eCos-based models (the BCM3380, BCM3383 and BCM33834), where he found no usable fix and calls the bug a permanent "forever day," meaning a flaw that will never be patched on those devices, and newer Linux-based models (the BCM3390, BCM65xx and BCM68xx), which could be fixed if their makers switch Wi-Fi software.

In Belgium, Kaiser found the flaw present and exploitable on gateways from three of the four big providers: Proximus, Orange Belgium and VOO. A fourth, Telenet, may be affected too, but he could not test one.

A wider list he published, ranging from Cisco small-business access points to Huawei and ARRIS routers, mixes confirmed and unconfirmed entries, and some rest on an automated check that only flags a device as "likely vulnerable."

The Belgian per-provider counts, he says, run into the hundreds of thousands of gateways, but are rough estimates.

Why There's No Patch, and No CVE

The flaw is old. Kaiser traces the code back to at least 2010 and says Broadcom shipped an incomplete fix in 2018, then told customers to switch to a different Wi-Fi software package, called hostapd, rather than relying on the fix. On the older eCos chips, he says, no working fix was ever shipped, which is why he calls it a forever day.

No CVE, the tracking identifier that lets defenders and vendors follow a flaw, has been assigned to it. Kaiser says Broadcom told him it has known about the bug since 2018 and had heard about it from others, but would not register a CVE or say anything publicly, which he believes is why so many device makers never patched.

When he took the case to the CERT Coordination Center, it was closed the same day, because Broadcom itself holds the authority to assign CVEs for its products and would not do so. The Hacker News found no CVE for the flaw as of October 19.
